newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper says strike talks to resume.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper says strike talks to resume.

text.p: Colombian President Ernesto Samper said on Friday that talks to end a nationwide strike by public sector workers would resume this weekend and that he hoped a negotiated settlement could be reached soon.
"We hope to find a way out of this that is satisfactory to everyone," said Samper, who spoke to reporters during a visit to the northwest province of Cordoba.
"We've always been willing to find a solution but it has to be respectful of the government's legal and constitutional budgetary restrictions," he added.

Marathon talks aimed at ending the four-day-old strike ended in a deadlock early on Friday after the government refused to budge on its plan to raise public sector wages by an average of no more than 13.5 percent this year.
Union leaders representing 800,000 state workers across the country are insisting on a 21.5 percent pay hike to compensate for inflation of more than 21 percent last year.
The government, which is fighting to plug a gaping fiscal deficit, has said it was unable to improve on its offer.
But Samper said he had ordered Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo and other government officials to come up with new "economic formulas" that could help satisfy union demands.
"New contacts (with union leaders) will be made this weekend," he said.

Luis Eduardo Garzon, head of the country's leading labour group, the Unitary Workers' Confederation, said earlier that the government had basically killed off any hope of a negotiated settlement by refusing to cede ground on the wage issue.
"We'll only return (to the bargaining table) if the government modifies its offer substantially," he said.

There have been conflicting reports on the impact of the strike, which prompted mass protests in Bogota and other leading cities on Thursday as workers took to the streets to back demands for wage hikes and and an end to planned privatisations.
Ocampo said early on Friday that the government had ruled out any possibility of altering its privatisation plans, but he hinted that it might be willing to improve on its wage offer.
Union officials say they have succeeded in disrupting key economic and social sectors, including oil, telecommunications, education and all but emergency health care.
But the government maintains that only 10 percent of state workers have heeded the strike call and that schools and universities are the only sector that have been seriously affected.

Despite threats from National Liberation Army rebels to provided "armed support" for the work stoppage, and government warnings that leftist guerrillas were trying to infiltrate the strike movement, no serious violence has been reported since it began at midnight on Monday.
